conclusion: The full January2026 CE1045A and relevant complete 2026 fee tables are now actually read. They distinguish inspection, certificate and administration categories. Selecting the actual category and complete project bill requires the real space/use facts, rather than another generic fee-source retrieval.

sections.heading: Start with the exact unit and proposed use
paragraphs: A Certificate of Occupancy (CO) must be obtained before a covered commercial building or individual lease space is occupied. The city’s existing-building brochure excludes single-family residences and U-occupancies from its stated building-code requirement. Check the exact unit’s record and whether your operation changes the occupancy classification; changed classification requires approved plans and permits for a new CO.
Describe relevant storage, chemicals, powered equipment and public access. The city lists building, fire, food and other reviews, but that does not make every permit mandatory for every business.

sections.heading: Apply through the existing-building inspection route
paragraphs: The city’s CE-1278 brochure directs an existing-building or lease-space applicant to email form CE1045A or CE1045B to Occupancy.Inspections@houstontx.gov, or submit the documents in person at the Houston Permitting Center. It lists the supporting declaration, current Texas or U.S. photo identification, full business address and telephone number, approximate area and floors, and present/proposed and previous business type if known. A new business must give its name. Multiple-building sites need the specified site map; apartments need building and unit counts.

The inspection team records discrepancies. Its report identifies structural, electrical, mechanical or plumbing corrections and whether separate permits are needed before work. The brochure gives 180 days to obtain required permits and complete corrections. An owner or agent may obtain a required structural permit; electrical, mechanical and plumbing permits require a licensed contractor. Only the permit holder or licensed contractor can request inspections for that permitted work.

sections.heading: Budget for the inspection as well as the certificate
paragraphs: The 2026 fee schedule lists $537.12 for the first-story Certificate of Occupancy or life-safety inspection category. The January 2026 application separately lists a $94 CO fee on all applications and says a $33.56 administration fee per application is not included. Looking only at the certificate charge can understate the opening budget.

The space changes the inspection category: additional floors or a large area can add charges. Individual retail or office spaces under 3,000 square feet in multi-tenant buildings have a separate category; its rate also changes when the inspection is performed alongside the building-core inspection. Other permitted work or a warranted investigation can add charges. Use the city’s assessment of the actual project rather than treating one listed amount as the complete bill.

sections.heading: Corrections and final approval come before the certificate
paragraphs: After repairs and final inspections are approved, the October 2024 brochure says the CO is emailed automatically to the application address; it is not mailed. Its 180-day correction period does not replace the requirement to obtain the CO before occupancy. If an existing, unmodified space’s CO cannot be located, the brochure describes obtaining a duplicate instead.
The required application category, combined charges and the city’s assessment of the actual property remain separate.

sections.heading: What to establish before relying on the space
paragraphs: Check the parcel, address and unit: the Houston metro, Harris County and City of Houston are not interchangeable. A mailing address or landlord’s account of the previous tenant does not settle the responsible authority or proposed use.

Resolve the applicable occupancy and inspection questions before relying on the date at which rent, equipment orders or customer promises create costs. You may model a delay to understand exposure, but it is not the city’s promised timetable or a legally required lease clause.

limitations: This is the city’s CE-1278 existing-building/no-change-of-use route, the January 2026 CE-1045-A form and the named 2026 fee categories. It is not the full new-construction, changed-use or every business-opening process.

The actual municipal boundary, use classification, other building/fire/environmental/sector permissions, required corrections and complete city invoice depend on the project. The separate multifamily CE1045B form is not reviewed here.
guidePatch.description: Follow Houston’s existing-building occupancy inspection route and separate the inspection charge, certificate fee and administration fee before budgeting to open.

sections.heading: Which fact changed?
paragraphs: The official page lists first use, tenant change on an existing CO, changed use and changed floor area among new-Certificate-of-Occupancy triggers. Obtain the previous CO for the exact unit and describe the incoming company, work, equipment, storage and area.

Submit the application and Land Use Questionnaire through DallasNow with the appropriate fee. The city says changed-use requests go to Building Code and Zoning review and may need site, floor or parking information. For the same use, inspections can be scheduled after approval and payment. The CO is released after all required inspections pass; payment does not guarantee approval.

sections.heading: A name-only change has a published application route
paragraphs: For a trading-name change, the specific city FAQ says to submit a standalone Certificate of Occupancy application through DallasNow and describe the change clearly, for example “Updating DBA to XYZ Company”. DBA means “doing business as”. Staff then review whether supporting documents are needed; approval produces a new CO.

The city calls a pure DBA-only change a record change, and its currently linked fee schedule lists a $30 Record Change Fee, separately from the $375 general CO permit fee. For multifamily uses, this option requires no recorded code violations; otherwise the city calls for a new CO and building inspections.

A standalone application does not by itself establish which fee category applies. Final fees are assessed for the actual submission. A new legal tenant is a separate trigger, and the FAQ does not promise that every requested change avoids inspection.

limitations: Dallas occupancy guidance and the currently linked fee schedule, effective July1,2025, are reviewed for the named routes and categories. The city determines the actual category, supporting documents, inspections, charges and opening permission. This is not a Texas-wide rule or a complete trade/employment/tax/franchise review.

sections.heading: The difference worth checking
paragraphs: Dallas lists tenant change on an existing Certificate of Occupancy (CO) as a new-certificate trigger. San Antonio describes an update for certain owner/lessee changes with essentially the same use, but listed categories still need a new certificate. Both describe new-CO requirements for changed business use.

For a name-only change, Dallas’s specific FAQ directs a standalone DallasNow CO application. Its currently linked fee schedule lists a $30 Record Change category separately from the general CO permit fee; the city assesses the actual submission. Multifamily properties with recorded violations instead need a new CO and building inspections. San Antonio’s linked DBA (doing business as) form requires fire review and inspection for specified uses, including repair and maintenance shops, and applies the COO-No Construction fee category. Neither the word “update” nor an application format proves that the chosen site needs no inspection or has a lower total charge.
Request the prior CO and actual operator/use facts for the chosen unit, then continue with that city’s guide. This comparison cannot choose a use classification, inspection route or opening date.

limitations: Two-city comparison only, not a Texas-wide rule. Actual site/use, legal operator and construction/fire/trade conditions still matter. Published fee categories do not establish which charge or inspection route either city will assign to an actual request.

No numerical total-cost or opening-time advantage is established between the cities.
